question: The boss pulled him off his own presentation to make him take notes instead. What pattern does this reflect?
options: Assuming administrative/support work belongs to him regardless of what he'd earned or prepared
A random scheduling mix-up with no deeper pattern
A performance issue with his previous work
A rotation system every employee goes through equally

question: He said, "Actually, I'd really like to present. I've prepared extensively." What happened to that boundary?
options: It was brushed off with "cute" and overridden without any real consideration
It was respected and he got to present after all
It was discussed calmly and a compromise was reached
He never actually stated it out loud

question: When the whole room laughed at his "sonion rings" slip, Linda was the one who pointed it out. What would ethical bystander behavior have looked like instead?
options: Someone redirecting the moment rather than piling onto the laughter
Waiting for him to laugh at himself first
Recording the moment to bring up in his performance review
Nothing — reacting to an honest mistake is fine

question: He ends the scene thinking, "Just once in my life I'd like to go an entire day without having a bruh moment." What does this reveal, and what response would help?
options: A pattern of repeated small humiliations — someone acknowledging that pattern would help more than brushing off one moment
He's overreacting to a single joke and should let it go
Nothing needs to happen; this is normal workplace banter
He should be told to develop a thicker skin
